published.title: The Harvest Before the Rain
published.body:
A Parable of Faith, Obedience, and Surrender

In the valley of Shiloah, where the earth was often stubborn and the rains were fickle, lived a farmer named Wafi, known to the seekers of the valley as Elian.

To his neighbors, he was Wafi—the loyal, the steadfast. But to those who saw the light of conviction in his eyes, he was Elian, a man whose very existence seemed to be an extension of his relationship with the Divine.

The two names reflected different aspects of the same man. Wafi was the man who faithfully worked the land; Elian was the man whose heart belonged entirely to Yahweh. Yet neither identity existed apart from the other. His devotion was revealed through his labor, and his labor was sustained by his devotion.

While other men in the village spent their evenings pacing their porches, calculating the risks of the wind, or cursing the dryness of the soil, Wafi slept the sleep of a child.

One year, a great drought gripped the land. The river shrank to a silver thread, and the clouds teased the valley with shadows but never delivered a drop. The other farmers grew frantic. They hoarded their remaining grain, arguing in the town square about who had failed the heavens or which ritual would bring back the rain.

Wafi, however, spent his days in the heat, bowing his back to the dust. He planted his seeds deeply, one by one, in soil that looked like powdered ash.

His neighbors laughed, calling him a fool.

“You are burying your future in a grave, Wafi!” they shouted. “Look at the sky! There is no water. Your effort is a waste of sweat.”

Wafi stopped his plow and looked at them with eyes that held a peace they couldn’t comprehend. He didn’t argue or boast. He simply whispered:

“I do not plant for the rain; I plant for the Promise.”

Then he returned to his work.

Day after day, he continued planting. When the heat became unbearable, he rested beneath the shade of an old olive tree. When his hands blistered, he wrapped them in cloth and returned to the field. When the winds scattered dust across the furrows he had carefully prepared, he patiently cleared them again.

He never claimed to know when the rain would come. Nor did he claim that his fields would surely flourish.

He simply believed that obedience was not a transaction in which he performed a task to receive a reward. It was an expression of love—a relationship in which he offered his labor to Yahweh without demanding an outcome.

His faith was not a desperate wish or a bargain with Heaven. It was a firm conviction forged through the study of the Word and a lifetime of trusting the One he could not see.

He understood that his responsibility was to plant faithfully. Whether the seeds flourished or remained buried beneath the dust, the outcome belonged to the Creator.

Each night, as the sun dipped behind the jagged hills, Wafi would wash the dust from his hands and kneel beside his bed.

He did not demand a miracle. Instead, he prayed in gratitude that he had been chosen to be a steward of the earth. He thanked Yahweh for the strength to be obedient and the grace to be still.

Sometimes he prayed for rain, as any farmer would. But he never allowed the absence of rain to become the measure of Yahweh’s faithfulness.

For Wafi had settled something within his heart long before the drought had settled upon the valley:

He would trust Yahweh whether the heavens opened or remained silent.

While the rest of the village lay awake, their minds racing with anxiety and their hearts heavy with doubt, Wafi closed his eyes.

He fell into a deep, rhythmic slumber, his breathing steady and his heart quiet.

He slept peacefully because he knew that the God who commanded the seed to grow in darkness was the same God who watched over him in the night.

He had done what was his to do. What remained was beyond his control, and he had surrendered it willingly.

The days became weeks.

The earth cracked beneath the relentless sun. Even the oldest villagers struggled to remember a season so unforgiving. Some farmers abandoned their fields entirely. Others stood at the edges of their land, staring toward the horizon, waiting for a sign that it was safe to begin.

Yet each morning, Wafi rose and tended the ground.

One evening, as the village prepared for another restless night, a low rumble rolled across the valley.

The sky turned a bruised purple. A cool wind swept through the narrow streets, carrying the scent of distant rain.

Then the heavens opened.

It was not a gentle rain but a deluge—a great outpouring that soaked the thirsty earth to its very marrow.

The rain continued through the night, filling the streams, softening the hardened fields, and awakening the valley from its long season of thirst.

When morning came, Wafi stepped outside and looked upon the rain-soaked earth.

He smiled, knelt beside the nearest furrow, and offered a quiet prayer of thanksgiving.

But he did not celebrate as though he had earned the rain.

He knew it was a gift.

In the days that followed, the valley slowly transformed.

Small green shoots began breaking through the softened soil. Where other farmers had waited too long to plant, fearing the risk, much of the land remained bare.

But in Wafi’s field, life was stirring.

The seedlings grew with extraordinary vigor. Their roots reached deeply into the earth, and their leaves stretched toward the heavens. What had once appeared to be a field of buried hopes became a sea of living green.

The weeks passed, and the crops flourished beyond anything the valley had witnessed in generations.

By harvest time, the fields shimmered gold beneath the afternoon sun.

The harvest was not merely a success; it was a multiplication.

Wafi’s barns overflowed—not because he had commanded the heavens, nor because his obedience had obligated Yahweh to reward him, but because the Creator had chosen to bring abundance from the seeds he had faithfully planted.

And Wafi understood something the villagers had not yet learned.

Had the rain never come, his obedience would not have been wasted.

Had the harvest failed, Yahweh would still have been worthy of his trust.

For the true measure of his faith had never been the fullness of his barns, but the condition of his heart.

As the villagers gathered to marvel at the golden fields, they asked him the secret of his courage.

“How did you know the rain would come?” one farmer asked.

“How could you rest when everything around us was dying?” asked another.

Wafi smiled, looking up at the vast blue expanse.

For a moment, he was no longer simply Wafi, the steadfast farmer whom his neighbors had known for years. They began to recognize the spirit of Elian—the man whose trust in Yahweh had remained unshaken even when the earth beneath his feet had failed him.

“I did not know the rain would come,” he answered gently. “And I did not know whether my seeds would live or die.”

The villagers fell silent.

“I knew only that I had been given a field to tend and seeds to plant. So I planted. And when my work was finished, I entrusted what I could not control to the Father.”

He paused, allowing his words to settle upon them.

“The secret is not in the seed or the rain. The secret is in the sleep.”

The villagers looked at one another, struggling to understand.

Wafi continued:

“When you truly trust the heart of the Father, you understand that the burden is surrendered the moment you obey. You may still have fields to tend, hardships to endure, and seasons of waiting ahead. But you no longer need to carry tomorrow’s worries as though they belong to you.”

He looked toward the golden fields and smiled once more.

“Had the rain never come, I would still have slept. For my peace was never found in the promise of a harvest, but in the faithfulness of the One who holds the harvest in His hands.”

And as the evening sun settled over the valley of Shiloah, the villagers began to understand.

The greatest miracle was not that a barren field had produced an abundant harvest.

It was that, long before the first drop of rain had fallen, a man had already found his rest in Yahweh.

published.title: The Empty Chair
published.body:
Every Sunday, an elderly woman named Margaret sat in the same pew at church. Beside her was an empty chair.

For years, her husband had occupied that seat. After he passed away, she continued saving it.

One morning, a young man entered the church looking defeated. He stood near the entrance, unsure where to sit.

Margaret noticed him and smiled.

"There's a place right here," she said, pointing to the empty chair.

The young man sat beside her.

After the service, he admitted that he had almost given up on life. He had walked into the church hoping to find a reason to keep going.

Margaret gently took his hand.

"Sometimes God leaves a space in our lives because someone else is going to need it."

That Sunday, the chair wasn't empty anymore.

And neither was Margaret's heart.

published.title: The Weight We Carry
published.body:
A man walked along a quiet road carrying a heavy backpack filled with stones.

Every stone represented something he refused to release.

One was regret.

Another was anger.

Others carried the names of people who had hurt him.

As the miles passed, his shoulders grew tired and his steps became slower.

Eventually, he stopped beside a river.

He opened the backpack and examined each stone.

For the first time, he asked himself why he was still carrying things that belonged to yesterday.

One by one, he placed the stones beside the water.

He couldn't change what had happened.

He couldn't rewrite the past.

But he could decide what he carried into tomorrow.

When he stood again, the road hadn't changed.

The distance ahead was still the same.

But his journey had become lighter.

Sometimes healing begins when we finally put something down.

published.title: The Light in the Window
published.body:
Every evening, a little girl watched her father turn on the porch light.

"Why do you leave it on all night?" she asked.

Her father smiled.

"So anyone trying to find their way home can see where they're going."

Years passed, and the little girl grew older.

Eventually, she moved away and experienced the difficulties of adulthood.

There were moments when life felt overwhelming and she wondered whether she had lost her way.

One evening, after a particularly difficult day, she returned to her childhood home.

As she turned onto the familiar street, she noticed something.

The porch light was still shining.

Her father was waiting at the door.

She realized that the light had never been about electricity.

It was about love.

It was about hope.

It was about knowing that no matter how dark the journey became, there was still somewhere she belonged.

And perhaps that's what faith is.

A light that remains on, even when we cannot see the road.
